speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a rather extraordinary procedure. I presume it is possible and in order to move that the report be concurred in. Is it competent for a committee that has made a final report -which I understand the committee had made previous to the report now before us-to come back to the house and amend that final re-ipont? speechtext:
I think the point of order raised by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), regarding the amendment to the third and final report of the committee is well taken. The most practical way to amend this report is to refer it back to the committee with instructions that they have the power to reduce the number of printed copies from 10,000 to 1.000. I suggest to the mover (Mr. McIntosh) that he amend his motion-I do not think he will have any difficulty in getting the unanimous consent of the house, because it is an unimportant point-on the lines above indicated. The committee can be reconvened and can bring in a report with a view to reducing the number of printed copies from 10,000 to 1,000. The following ruling is given in Bourinot, page 480, and Beauchesne, paragraph 661:
When the motion is proposed the report may he referred back to the committee for further consideration or with instruction to amend the same in any respect. It is not competent for a committee to reconsider and reverse its own decision, but if the house resolves that such reconsideration is necessary, the correct procedure is for the house to give the committee instructions which will enable it to consider the whole question again.
Motion stands.

The house resumed, from Monday, May 2S, consideration of the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) for committee of supply, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Bourassa:
The house regrets that proper steps have not yet been taken to give full effect, both in domestic and external affairs, to the "equality of status" acknowledged by the Imperial conference, 1926, to be the "root-principle" of the relationship between the self-governing Britannic communities.
['Order.\nProgress reported.']

Mr. Speaker, last night I spoke on this question from half past ten to eleven o'clock; I will do my utmost in the house to defeat this amendment in the other ten minutes at my disposal. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) is moving this particular amendment for political purposes and to gain votes in the province of Quebec. He wants to make political capital out of the British Empire which he has been making a football of for many a day now. Canada is not going to be talked out of the British Empire. If Canada could be talked out of the British Empire, the hon. member for Labelle would have done that long ago. Canada is not going to be talked out of the British Empire; Canada will have to be fought out of the British Empire. Canada is not going to be written out of the British Empire by the Dafoes, the Atkinsons, the Ewarts and all the rest of the gentlemen of that separatist description. The hon. member for Labelle and his illustrious leader are two souls with but a single thought, two hearts that beat as one on this particular equality of status question.
I did not start this discussion. As I say, it was started for political purposes by the hon. member for Labelle. He has found the session rather barren of results so far as the government is concerned in regard to solving

Foreign Relations-Mr. Church
the economic ills of the country, and so he has to trot forward this problem in which he refers to the government of the old country as our imperial masters, or the imperial monster who is seeking to devour all Canada, The Imperial conference, in my opinion, has left undone those things which it ought to have done and done those things which it ought not to have done and there was no health in it. No results came out of it so far as the overseas dominions were concerned. Like the League of Nations it has created more confusion and set up more strife than ever. We are proud that Canada is an integral part of the greatest empire the world has ever known. The war left us our status as it was. What Canada has done during the past thirty-five years she has done of her own volition, and' voluntarily, and she would do the same thing again, namely, come to the mother country's aid in her hour of peril. So the people of this country are satisfied with our present status and seek no change in it. Far better for Canada would it have been had the Imperial conference solved our economic problems-trade, defence and migration-instead of all this status talk.
After all is said and done the Prime Minister is only following the footsteps of Sir Robert Borden because he was the archconspirator in connection with the change of status. In 1919 at the treaty of Versailles Sir Robert Borden insisted that Canada should sign that treaty separately. He also insisted on Canada having a separate seat in the League of Nations. It would have done Canada as much if not more good for good will and peace if he had insisted on our having a seat in the American baseball league or the national and international league. It would be as practical as the League of Nations. As regards our status what have we secured and what has been the change in chronological order? In 1919 there was the treaty of Versailles which was signed separately. In 1921 there was the Washington Disarmament conference. When Sir Robert Borden and Sir George Foster brought up in the house the question of an ambassador to Washington and put it through, if I had been the only Conservative in the house at the time I would have opposed such a proposition to divide Britain's representation at Washington which was the beginning of all this monument of folly known as separatism.
In March, 1923, the Halibut treaty was signed at Washington separately by Mr. Lapointe. In 1923 the Imperial conference confirmed the separate signing of treaties. In 1924 Canada acted separately in the conference on the Dawes plan. Then there was the
question of the reservation of Dominion legislation for the assent of His Majesty or for the disallowance of such legislation. The hon. member for Labelle says now that the disallowance of legislation by His Majesty is all a matter of form. He says that the Colonial Laws Validity Act was invoked not long ago by the Privy Council to annul a statute of Canada; that this statute was wiped out by a stroke of the pen because of its possible application to Ireland. If they can wipe off the statute books that act which is the foundation of all the charters of liberty of the overseas dominions, they can change our new status and wipe the British North America Act off the statute books by a stroke of the pen also and repeal the British North America Act. In this way they can interfere with the rights of the provinces, with the rights of minorities, with the rights of municipalities in this country, and with the right of one minority to have its own religion and laws and preservation of its language. We are thus at the parting of the ways. No one knows where it will all land us.
In 1926 the conference recognized the right of each dominon to make separate and independent treaties not binding on any other dominion. We are a separate country. We have sovereign power. The people of the United States admit that. They have sent us what is known as the Kellogg note about peace and war with a general presidential election in the near future. While Secretary Kellogg on one side of the capitol is inviting the nations of the world to join in a collective renunciation of war, Secretary Wilbur is being voted the sum of $274,000,000 for the building, during the next three years, of fifteen cruisers at a cost of seventeen million dollars each and an aeroplane-carrier at nineteen million dollars. Mr. Kellogg's colleague asked for twenty-five of these 10,000-ton cruisers, but Congress thought fifteen of them in the next three years would be enough to go on with. Especially with the elections so near! [DOT]
The governor general is a mere viceroy. If he appealed to Downing street for advice he would be told: We have nothing to do with you; you are over in Canada alone and your cabinet there alone can advise you. In 1927 we won a seat in the League of Nations. What good that seat is to us, I do not know except that there will be a nice little trip between sessions for this minister or that minister and an expense account for living allowance as well. The academic league has now cost the people of this country $1,800,090 all told and has been barren of results to Canada and created more strife than peace.

Foreign Relations-Mr. Church
In 1927 we went into the ambassador business and Canada now proposes to send ambassadors to Japan and France. The United States and France and England are to send ambassadors to Canada. Did you ever hear the like of it? Where will all this separatism end? Where is it all going to land Canada? It simply means that the so-called "evolution" in theory and practice is working out in the best interests of complete separation in both domestic and external affairs. This evolution has become and is working out as a peaceful revolution. That is all that equality of status and separatism have done for Canada. The next step will come gradually and surely, namely, to change and to do the British North America Act to death and we are by this status setting up a new constitution in the name of evolution. Our separation now is as complete in a peaceful way as that of old of the North American colonies. That is the gist of it all in plain practice. No wonder the government want to close up this debate and not startle the country any further seeing that this status has landed us in a state of uncertainty and doubt and division and separation from the motherland. As a separate country we now are to be mixed up in all the foreign politics of Europe, Asia and America, for are we not boasting that way? We are at the parting of the ways. Whither are we drifting? No wonder even government members are beginning to wag their heads in doubt as to where we are, and to get alarmed at the huge cost of it all to Canada.
I say in conclusion the government want to close off this debate, because of its effect on the people of British descent of this country, who now only comprise fifty-five per cent of the population of this country. It is no wonder that many members as well as supporters of the government are wagging their heads and wondering where this equality of status folly is going to land Canada. So _ far as that goes, we are now at the parting of the ways, and we do not know what the next step is going to be. We still continue to sponge on the mother country for our defence both on land and sea. The people whom I have the honour to represent have no more pride in the nation-builders of their own party than I have in the nation builders of the party opposite. I have no use for the nation building that Sir Robert Borden, the Hon. Wedley Rowell, and the other oracles of Union government pretended to do at Versailles and WaAington. I have no use for the nation wrecking separatism of Sir Robert Borden's proposal to establish a Cana-

dian embassy at Washington. That embassy is not now and never wil be anything in the nature of a centre of service for the good of Canada. The embassy at Washington is a sink hole, and the Canadian high commissioner's office at London is not much better. These embassies, or sink holes, as I call them, will be duplicated all over the earth by this government. When the seed planted by Sir Robert Borden's and the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King's separatist embassy at Washington has reached maturity, what will the harvest be? The harvest will be reaped by the taxpayers of Canada. That harvest wil not be in the form of crops that will fill their barns, ibuit ft. will be in the form of taxes that will empty their pockets. Canada will then be spending two or three million dollars per annum in interest and debt charges on embassy buildings .and on the salaries and upkeep of useless Canadian ambassadors, and still more useless Staffs of clerks. Canada must spend two or three million dollars per annum in order to prove that we are in an academic way a nation without a navy or an army.
Never in the entire history of Canada has she at any time been alble to defend herself. We are a nation only in a mythical and academic sense.
No matter what the Imperial conference says or does, our representatives have no right to take away our birthright in this way on the pretence of evolution. It means we are a separate sovereign state independent of Great Britain, and without any semblance of a navy or army to help us.
That is what the resolution of the hon. member for Labelle means. I hope that he will not have the privilege of withdrawing his motion; I hope that unanimous consent will not foe given to allowing him to withdraw it, but that it will be pressed to a division so that the people of this country will at last awake to where this equality of status is landing Canada-out of the British Empire sooner or later.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take the time of the house except for a very few minutes. On several occasions I have expressed my views on certain phases of the report of the Imperial conference of 1926. In expressing those views I paid particular attention to certain clauses of that report which I thought were over-emphasized by the Prime Minister when the report was first under discussion, and I think certain of those clauses have been over-emphasized in the discussion in the South African parliament and also in the parliament of the Irish Free State.

Foreign Relations-Mr. Cahan
If one reads that report and endeavours to place himself in the atmosphere in which it was negotiated, may I say, and finally accepted, I believe that there was, upon the part of the majority of tihe prime ministers and their associates representing the several dominions at the Imperial conference, a sincere desire to preserve in our time, and' for future time, so far as possible, the unity of the British Empire, which they therein described as the British commonwealth of nations. I am sure, from the addresses of several members to which I have listened from time to time in this house, and particularly the addresses which the Prime Minister has given here and in various parts of the country, that he has a supreme desire to preserve the unity of this British eomonwealth-the political unity, imay I say, of this British commonwealth. But in preserving the unity of the eomonwealth it was necessary for those who were representing this dominion and the other dominions at the last Imperial conference to take into consideration what I might call the peculiar views or idiosyncrasies of the representatives of one or more of the dominions there represented, who had never had the experience in constitutional growth and practice which we have enjoyed for sixty years in this dominion; and I can well appreciate that, in order to satisfy their fears and anticipations for the future, particularly sitrong emphasis was laid by the draftsmen of that report upon the autonomy of the several dominions composing this British commonwealth.
But it seems to me that the problem which these representatives then had before them was a problem similar to that which faced the representatives of the dominions at the Imperial war conference of 1917, where in referring to the proposed readjustment of the constitutional relations of the component parts of the empire, they placed on record their view that:
Any such readjustment should recognize the right of the dominions and of India to an adequate voice in foreign policy and in foreign relations, and should provide effective arrangements for continuous consultation in all important matters of imperial concern, and for such necessary concerted action founded on consultation as the several governments may determine.
I think that the problem of the representatives of the several!: dominions at the Imperial conferences from that time down to the present has been to provide for this dominion as well as for the other dominions an adequate voice in foreign policy and in foreign relations. 'Some differences of opinion may exist as to what is an adequate voice, but the position reached by common agreement at the last Imperial conference seems to be this: That each dominion in respect of these foreign relations which solely and exclusively apply to its own interests shall' in the future be represented by its own ministry, and represented by its own agents, whoever they may be, who are duly accredited for the negotiation of treaties dealing with matters that are peculiarly and solely and exclusively of interest to such dominion. Therefore, the Imperial conference of 1926 approved of the appointment of a special minister by -Canada accredited to the government at Washington. We are in a most peculiar situation with regard to our neighbours to the south. They have a population of over one hundred millions of people, and they are conscious of their vast material1 and financial resources, and confident of their political power. We, on the other hand, are a small country of less than ten million people, and we, too, are conscious of our own special rights. Two peoples living alongside a common boundary stretching for three thousand miles between them, having these peculiar characteristics, must face from time to time many problems 'which we at least who are of the smaller nation must regard as of vital importance to our present and our future interests.
There was too in this country a sentiment which had been propagated for many years, and with which I do not wholly coincide, that our rights had been sacrificed from time to time since the earliest treaties were made between Great Britain and the United States dealing with Canadian interests. It seems to me in surveying the history of the past that if Canadian agents had solely and exclusively directed the negotiation of those treaties, in view of our political position, in view of our lack of financial and material resources, in view of our very modest political power, they would have found it very difficult indeed to secure such advantageous terms as were secured from time to time by British representatives at Washington in consultation with the representatives of this country.
But that opinion prevailing throughout the length and breadth of this land had at least to be conciliated, and therefore it has been provided that Canada, in regard to the United States particularly, shall have her own minister at Washington, and that those matters which are of interest solely and exclusively to Canada shall be negotiated and administered by the representative of Canada at Washington. But the correspondence, as I stated on another occasion, which resulted in the appointment of a representative of Canada at Washington, following the appointment of a

Foreign Relations-Mr. Cahan
representative of the Irish Free State, clearly discloses the understanding which was reached between the government of Canada and the
government at Westminster to be this: that all matters in which Canada is solely and exclusively interested should be attended to by her own minister; but that when matters arise which may affect Great Britain herself and other parts of the empire, the minister representing Canada should always act in close association with the British ambassador at Washington, and that if the general interests of the British commonwealth are affected, the ambassador of Great Britain would in fact retain a predominating position.
When I look also at the resolutions of the conference of 1923,' which were submitted to and approved by this house, and the explanations made in reference thereto on June 21, 1926, by the Prime Minister of the day, I find ' that he invited parliament to pass _ a resolution to the effect that those treaties which impose active obligations upon Canada, and those treaties alone, should necessarily be presented for approval by the parliament of Canada before this government should advise His Majesty to ratify them in Canada's behalf. The words of the Prime Minister were clear; he said:
The present government by this resolution is asking parliament to approve of a course of procedure which will involve with respect to treaties, involving military and economic sanctions, the approval of parliament before the government of the day agrees to any obligation implied in the treaty being undertaken in the name of the country.
That resolution, after being so explained, passed this house unanimously. Therefore so long as that resolution remains in force and effect it would be unconstitutional on the part of the government of Canada to advise the ratification of a treaty binding upon Canada which imposed active obligations of the kind mentioned without first receiving the endorsement of this parliament. But that does not apply to a large body of treaties made with foreign states which do not involve active economic or military obligations. For instance, we have had before us during this session a number of conventions-which are really treaties-and this parliament has been asked to approve thereof by resolution. There is the slavery convention, the convention protocol of the second opium conference, the international sanitary convention-these all affect very intimately the Tights and obligations in many respects of Canada and of Canadian citizens. In view of the position

which this government has taken at a recent date, I was somewhat surprised that we were not asked to confirm those treaties by acts of the Canadian parliament. During the discussion I asked either the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) or the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) if those treaties coming into effect on the advice of the Canadian government and ratified by His Majesty the King through his duly accredited representative, would make them a part of the public law of this Dominion. I received no answer, and I am still in doubt whether the government have pursued the really effective course. In respect of the Waterways treaty of 1909, it will be remembered that an act was passed by the parliament of Canada in 1911 not only confirming that treaty but empowering the government to carry it into effect. I find in looking back over our recent political history that a similar course has been followed with regard to other treaties affecting Canada. For instance, I find that chapter 46 of the statutes of Canada for the year 1921 is an act to authorize the ratification and carrying into effect of the protocol of the 16th day of December, 1920, accepting the statute of the Permanent Court of International Justice of December 13, 1920. The first section of that act reads:
The governor in council is authorized to advise that His Majesty be humbly moved to ratify on behalf of Canada the said protocol of the 16th day of December, 1920, in the manner thereby stipulated.
That was a complete confirmation by the parliament of Canada. The act also provides in section 2 as follows:
The governor in council is authorized to make such orders in council, regulations and nominations and to give such directions and notices, and to do and authorize such other acts and things as may appear to him necessary, proper or expedient on the part of Canada for carrying into effect the said protocol and the provisions of the aforesaid statute for the Permanent Court of International Justice.
In my opinion these conventions, which were submitted to us during the present session and approved by resolution only, should necessarily be confirmed by statute of this parliament in order to give the government of Canada full power and authority to carry their provisions into effect.
But leaving that apart, there is no doubt at the present time with regard to the authority and jurisdiction-shall I say?-of the government of the United Kingdom in negotiating treaties which apply to all parts of His Majesty's dominions and possessions. I do not see at the present time any restriction

Foreign Relations-Mr. Cahan
placed upon the negotiation of such treaties by the representatives of His Majesty's government at Westminster -which apply generally to the whole empire so long as they do not impose active economic and miltiary obligations upon any one of the dominions. It is obvious of course, in view of the position which the parliament of Canada has taken, that the government of this country cannot without the approval of this parliament constitutionally advise the ratification of treaties imposing such obligations upon it. There remains the negotiation of treaties which contain, if I may say so, passive obligations regulating rights as between ourselves and the foreign nations with whom we negotiate, the rights of our citizens in those foreign countries, rights affecting our commerce and trade, and the rest. And hereafter, under the present practice, it is left to the parliament of Canada, when any vital issue involving war arises, to decide as to what action we shall take under the circumstances and conditions which then prevail.
But to return for a moment. The provisions laid down by the conference of 1923 with respect to the negotiation of treaties provided for the separate negotiation of treaties by each dominion, but left it to the dominion then negotiating to decide as to whether the proposed treaty would affect the interests of Great Britain or of the other dominions. An amending provision, approved by the conference of 1926, provided moreover that each dominion when negotiating a treaty should first notify the government of the United Kingdom, and the governments of the other dominions respectively, of their intent and of the purport of the proposed treaty, and that upon receipt of sudh notification such other dominion government or the government of Great Britain should express its dissent with reasonable promptness. If no dissent is expressed, then the negotiating government may proceed to the conclusion of any treaty which does not impose active obligations upon any of the governments which are represented at the Imperial -conference. Under that provision, which I have briefly summarized, I think His Majesty the King, on the advice of the government of Great Britain, may proceed to negotiate treaties dealing with the rights of Canadian citizens in Asia or South America or Central America or elsewhere, and that so long as the government of Canada, upon receiving due notification of the purport and intent of these treaties, declines to intervene, it thereby tacitly acquiesces in the government of Great Britain negotiating such treaty, which will affect to that extent Canadian rights and interests ; provided always, of course, that it
does not impose what we have termed "active obligations." But if active obligations are proposed under the treaty being negotiated by His Majesty's ministers at Westminster, then the assent of each government must first be obtained. Therefore the existing provisions, as amended by the Imperial conference of 1926, still afford a wide discretion to the government of the United Kingdom under which that government may assume the acquiescence of any dominion that fails to express its views in regard to impending negotiations of which it may be notified. So that the citizens of this country may yet be bound through apathy and acquiescence. Take for instance the treaty of Lausanne to which reference has been made. In respect of the treaty of Lausanne and in respect of those provisions of the proposed treaty between Great Britain and Egypt, in so far as they do not impose active obligations on this country they may-under the present practice -and I think properly so-be negotiated by His Majesty's ministers at Westminster. And if the Canadian government, on being invited to participate, does not express any dissent, such treaty may be placed in operation by the ratification of His Majesty alone; because there still exist the prerogative power and authority of His Majesty the King to ratify treaties which apply to all parts of the empire. As to whose advice His Majesty may receive in respect of such ratification, that is of course a matter of constitutional practice. But in respect of the Lausanne treaty this government informed, on March 24, 1924, the government of the United Kingdom that it would not invite the Canadian parliament to concur in the ratification of that treaty.
And that-I am quoting the words, I think, of the Minister of External Affairs of Canada: -Without the approval of parliament they-[DOT]

-will not take exception to such course as His Majesty's government may deem it advisable to recommend.
In that case Canada assumed no active obligation, but took no exception to the ratification of that treaty, although it did impose, I might say, passive duties and obligations upon Canada, or at least upon Canadian citizens in Turkish territory and Canadian trade and commerce and property, located in Turkish territory or under the jurisdiction of the Turkish government. Therefore the treaty of Lausanne was thereupon ratified in

Foreign Relations-Mr. Cahan
the name of the king on the advice of the British government and became binding upon Canada without confirmation by the Canadian parliament. And it is binding still upon Canada and upon all Canadians, because in the year 1924 the parliament of the United Kingdom passed chapter VII of the British statutes of that year, the Treaty of Peace (Turkey) Act, 1924, an Act to Carry into Effect a Treaty Passed between His Majesty and Certain Other Powers, and Certain Conventions, Protocols, and Declarations connected Therewith. If hon. members will read the terms of that statute they will see that by section 1:
His Majesty may make such appointments, establish such offices, make such orders in council, and do such things as appear to him to be necessary for carrying out the said treaty, conventions, protocols and deliberation, and for giving effect to any of the provisions thereof.
And section 2:
Any order in council made under this act may provide for the imposition, by summary process or otherwise, of penalties in respect of breach of the provisions thereof, and for conferring on courts within His Majesty's dominions jurisdiction in cases where under the convention respecting conditions of residence and business and jurisdiction such courts are alone to have jurisdiction.
Therefore the treaty was not only ratified by His Majesty; it was approved by a statute of the parliament of Great Britain. His Majesty's government of Great Britain was authorized to carry out its full provisions; and the enforcement of penalties was placed as a duty and obligation upon Canadian courts by a statute of the Imperial parliament.
The Imperial conference of 1926 also specifically declared that any question as to whether the nature of a treaty was such that its ratification should be concurred in by all parts of the empire was a matter for discussion and agreement between their governments. I do not lay so much emphasis as the Prime Minister appeared to do the other day, on the fact that the Secretary of State for the United States at the suggestion of the British government sent a communication to this government in respect of the Kellogg peace proposals, because I am sure the Prime Minister of this country does not wish to act separately and independently from the governments of the other dominions and from the government of the United Kingdom in regard to these negotiations. I assume from the position which the Prime Minister took at the recent Imperial conference that he realizes the absolute necessity, if we are to preserve the existing unity of the empire, of consultation and concurrence wherever
fMr. Cahan.]
possible between the governments of the dominions and that of the United Kingdom with respect to matters which appertain to the whole empire to which we belong.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I have noticed that certain
gentlemen in this country who are admittedly in favour of the early independence of Canada and of breaking the light ties of association which bind us to Great Britain and the other dominions, speak of Canada having become in fact though not in name an independent and practically sovereign state. The Imperial conference of 1926 took an entirely different view; as I read it, and I have read it time and again, it seems to me that those who directed the drafting of that report were insisting that all matters which relate solely and exclusively to this Dominion should be under the sole and exclusive jurisdiction of the parliament and the administration of this country. So, in the negotiation of treaties, our minister or representative abroad, in those matters which relate solely and exclusively ito our interests and to our well-being, would have exclusive jurisdiction, but when our interests also become matters of interest to the other dominions, to the United Kingdom and to the empire as a whole, it is implied in the Imperial conference report that as far as it is possible for honourable and intelligent men so to do, those representing the various parts of this empire, should strive to reach a concurrent view by consultation and concession, so long as they make no sacrifice of the vital interests of any part, in order to promote the general interests of the autonomous dominions and of Great Britain.
That is my hope, because in my opinion there is no doubt that at present we 'have not the political strength which will enable us to stand alone as an independent sovereignty and protect the rights which we have so jealously guarded during the last sixty years. I wish to say nothing offensive to our great neighbours to t'he south, but especially is that fact true in view of the confidence and consciousness of that great republic that their political power and their financial and material strength are not only paramount on this continent but becoming paramount throughout the world. While personally I will be pleased to see representatives of this country, in the future as in the recent past, engaged in the negotiation of conventions and treaties for the settlement of difficulties and the solution of the problems which may arise between Canada and the United States, still I have a lingering belief that the co-operation, advice

Foreign Relations-Mr. Cahan
and assistance of the government of the United Kingdom and its ambassador at Washington may yet be of vital interest to us and to our success in such negotiations. Therefore I feel persuaded that the government of Canada, looking at the whole matter, though determined to preserve our autonomous rights, will always be equally determined to preserve the political unity of this empire to which we belong, believing that under present conditions and as far as human minds can see into the future, it is in the paramount interests of Canada that we should preserve that association with Great Britain and the other dominions.
On the other hand, why introduce an element of discord into this country? The speeches which have been made on various platforms throughout Canada, in which it has been suggested that we are an independent sovereign state, with the implication that we are about to pursue an independent course and separate from Great Britain, have really deeply wounded the sentiments of hundreds of thousands of thinking people throughout Canada. It is a fact which must be recognized, that a great body of our people, and they are not confined to one race, believe in maintaining that association and that bond of empire, however light it may be; they believe that the existing ties are more honourable to both great races in Canada than any other political alliance which we might now form with any other foreign power, that the existing political association is more compatible and more consistent with the best traditions of our forefathers, some of whom actually fought to establish the constitutional liberty of this country. Those thoughtful patriotic men who preceded us, endeavoured year by year and decade by decade to mould British institutions to adapt them to the particular needs of our country, and we have now attained a position in the British Empire which I am sure will enable us to have an adequate voice in all matters of imperial concern which affect our interests; a voice which as we grow in strength will, I hope, enable us to influence the foreign policy of that empire so that it may be more consistent, if that is possible, with the views entertained by the intelligent and patriotic citizens of this Dominion. I look forward' to the future when this Dominion, autonomous, it is true, will nevertheless influence in a large measure, by consultation, by advice and by co-operation, the future policy of the government of the United Kingdom and the governments of our associated dominions.
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to go into this question at greater length, but I suggest that in respect of those imperial statutes which were enacted years ago and which still apply to this country, the solution of our difficulties, if I may be allowed to say so, may be found to a large extent in adopting the policy recommended in the report of the last Imperial conference. It should be done, so far as possible, by concurrent legislation between the United Kingdom and the various dominions of the empire. It was by concurrent legislation that Canadian citizens born and bred, and Canadian citizens who had procured naturalization in this country, obtained the rights of natural born British citizens in every British community throughout the world. I am proud to say and glad to admit that the Imperial Naturalization Act of 1914 was based largely on the proposals made by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier at the Imperial conference of 1911.
I do not think that it detracts one iota from our status, that it detracts one iota from our dignity as self respecting British citizens, that when matters of general interest arise representatives of our government should enter into amicable negotiations with the government of the United Kingdom and the other dominion governments to devise reciprocal legislation which will assure to us, as Canadian citizens, all the rights of British citizens throughout the world, and thus ensure to us that protection-I am not merely talking of naval protection-which comes through the proper exercise of the political influence of a commonwealth such as ours.
I have had occasion to look into the statutes of the parliament of Great Britain which still apply to us, and, the longer I pursued my investigations, the more statutes and treaties I found which directly affect us. I would suggest to the government that when they come to consider the modification of these statutes they will find their ramifications so extensive as almost to appall them. Before the next Imperial conference this government should make haste slowly, and, by such expert assistance as is available, should probe these matters to the bottom. They should do this not with a view to organizing some method of taking this dominion out of'the commonwealth, but to devise ways and means by agreement and concurrent legislation, and, by new conventions where legislation is not necessary, for the purpose of keeping this Dominion within the British commonwealth. Let us keep Canada in the empire as a dominion fully conscious of its rights and privileges,

I should like to say a few words with regard to a certain matter that came to my notice when visiting London a year ago. While in London I took the opportunity of visiting both Canada House and the Australian building. I take it that we have this house in London to advertise Canada's business and Canada's wares as well as to encourage people to come to this country. Although I found Canada House an inviting place for Canadian visitors, very nicely equipped with rest rooms and writing rooms and attractive from the social point of view, at the same time, as compared with the house maintained by Australia in London, Canada

Supply-High Commissioner's Office
House seems to take second place. For instance, with regard to interesting people in Canada from an immigrant point of view- and when I say immigrant I take it to mean all classes of people who are coming to make their homes in Canada-I found there was nothing to draw attention to Canada except certain literature such as would be found in the office of any immigration agent. This might go to their houses through the mails just as well as by being put on a file at Canada House. Comparing Canada House with Australia House in London I find1 this difference, that in Australia House there is placed before the visitor a miniature picture of Australia. No doubt the Prime Minister himself has seen this as well as myself and indeed most members who have gone to London have taken the opportunity of visiting both these places. Not only do you find in Australia House an advertisement of their great mineral possibilities, agricultural resources and orchard production, but you have, as I say, a miniature picture before you of every state in the Commonwealth of Australia. Along with that you have of course literature similar to that which we have in Canada House. It seems to me that if we took a leaf out of Australia's book we might do a great, deal more with the money we are spending in London on Canada House. I found the High Commissioner doing his best to give visiting Canadians in London every opportunity to enjoy the social life of the city, and that sort of thing, which is all very nice, but I take it that the main object of Canada House is not only to interest business generally in Canadian affairs, but to interest people Who are thinking of emigrating, in the hope that they may find, in what they see at Canada House, sufficient inducement to cause them to make up their minds to come to Canada. I just throw out this suggestion because I think it is very essential from the Canadian point of view, in order to get returns from what we are spending in London, that we should change our method of advertising Canada in England.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I may say to my hon. friend, with reference to the contrast he points out between Australia House and Canada House, that there is a distinct difference between the manner in which Australia and Canada respectively carry out some of their services, for example, the work of immigration. All the immigration work of Australia is centered in London. The policy of Canada has been to have immigration offices scattered throughout the British Isles, in England, Scotland and Ireland. We have altoget.her some twenty-five immigration offices scattered through the British Isles, while with the exception of London there are none so far as Australia is concerned, their whole work being centered in the Australian building. That, I think, accounts in large degree for the difference in the advertising of Canada at the Canadian building to which my hon. friend has made reference. One going into the Australian building does see, as my hon. friend has pointed out, much that is representative of the different states in Australia. I question however, whether as many people who are thinking of emigrating to any of the British dominions would team of Canada through one office in London as learn of Canada through the different offices scattered throughout the British Isles.

I am well aware of the fact that we have various offices scattered throughout Great Britain, but at the same time we must remember that there are more people in the city of London than there are in the whole of Canada, and at very little expense, if any, I think we could do still more valuable advertising through making certain changes at Canada House.

I also visited Canada House last year, and I was struck by the paucity of Canadians in Canada House. One would have supposed that if anywhere in Britain one would find Canadians, it would be there. This session I asked a question-I have not it before me -now-as to the number of employees in Canada House who had either been born in Canada or had spent five years in this country, on the idea that if they had spent five -years in Canada they would rank as Canadians or have a knowledge of conditions in part at least of Canada. I figured the answer out to mean that only eleven per cent of the employees of Canada House were Canadians in this sense. I think in an institution presumably devoted entirely to the advertising of Canada and the getting of immigrants for Canada, it would be advisable if more Canadians were employed, even though it would cost a little more to 6end them over from here. I think they would be more likely to fill the objects for which the employees are there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend will recall that after the war there were a great many outstanding accounts due Canada, some of them matters of adjustment between the British treasury and our treasury. There were also the loans that had been made to Greece and Roumania, and there were numerous other important financial transactions which had not been finally adjusted. My hon. friend will agree with me that in the office as it was constituted at the time he was high commissioner, if he had had to rely exclusively upon the staff then there, he would have found it difficult to deal satisfactorily on behalf of Canada with these important transactions. When Mr. Larkin was appointed high commissioner, one of the first steps he took was to endeavour to settle these transactions and to obtain payment of the advances and loans that were made by Canada during the war period. He retained Colonel Reid Hyde for the purpose of assisting him, Colonel Hyde being an expert chartered accountant and a Canadian then residing in London in whose ability Mr. Larkin had entire confidence. Colonel Reid Hyde performed his services most satisfactorily. Under the direction of the high commissioner he discussed with the British treasury and with others the details of the outstanding accounts with the result that very large sums have been paid to the Canadian treasury in the short time that Mr. Larkin has been High Commissioner in London. I might mention, as an example, the Roumanian and Greek loans. The government of hon. gentlemen opposite advanced, I think, to Greece and Roumania something like $25,000,000 each, to enable

Supply*-High Commissioner's Office
them to purchase Canadian commodities of different kinds. The commodities were purchased, but we have been unable to get payment although our own money was advanced for the purpose of the purchase. Apparently up to the present there has been very little chance of getting payment of the principal; but by the co-operation of Colonel Reid Hyde under direction of the high commissioner we have at least succeeded in making an arrangement whereby interest will be secured to Canada until the whole of the principal is paid. Up to the present time I understand that about $9,000,000 has been paid into the treasury. That is a large sum, considering that it represents interest alone.
A gentleman of the technical and professional qualifications which Colonel Reid Hyde possesses is almost essential to the High Commissioner's office for dealing with matters of this kind. I might say that the question of appointing him as a permanent official, in view of his knowledge of the financial matters with which the High Commissioner's office is concerned, has been under consideration, and at a subsequent session the government may ask parliament to approve of the appointment of a financial comptroller-because that is really what the position required is -for the office of the High Commissioner. Mr. Pacaud's name has been mentioned. Mr. Pacaud is the head of the office under the high commissioner. But his duties do not relate primarily to financial affairs, and I think m}' hon. friend from his experience as High Commissioner would feel that it was in every way advisable for Canada to have on the staff some expert accountant who would give his whole time to these very important financial matters.

The Prime Minister seems to give all the credit to Colonel Reid Hyde for collecting money from Greece and Roumania. I wonder if Mr. Larkin, our High Commissioner, is not entitled to some of that credit? It seems to me he must be. "

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I was very
careful to say that Colonel Reid Hyde had acted in consultation with and under the direction of the High Commissioner. Unquestionably the credit is primarily due to Mr. Larkin, whose great financial ability is recognized not only in this country but throughout the world. However, as my hon. friend knows, in transactions of this kind a high commissioner would wish to have associated with him someone who is able to render professional services of an expert character and

who could attend to details. I have just been looking over the class of professional services rendered. They relate to the adjustment of accounts with the treasury, with the admiralty, with the board of trade, to conferences regarding Canada's share of reparations under the Dawes plan, to the adjustment of the Greek and Roumanian loans, and so on. These are all financial transactions and, as my hon. friend has said, we are fortunate in having as High Commissioner a gentleman of such great experience in financial matters as Hon. Mr. Larkin. Under his direction the office has been able in this short time to secure for Canada the payments to which I have referred.

I thank my hon. friend. Apparently he is suffering from a little personal pique this afternoon. Then I was informed that Mr. Pacaud was at lunch and could not see me. Next day he wrote me a very nice letter apologizing for the delay occasioned me and asking if I would call again. Unfortunately I did not get an opportunity of doing so. While I was there a gentleman came bustling in and everything was on the jump at once. Here wtas Colonel Reid Hyde, with all the gold-braided flunkeys of the Canada House, touching their caps and bowing and scraping to Colonel Reid Hyde. Colonel Reid Hyde has been attached to the High Commissioner's office in a wholly unnecessary capacity. He might have done some of these minor jobs .for the High Commissioner, but as the Prime Minister has said, it wias the High Commissioner's duty-and undoubtedly he did it-to carry out the major negotiations in connection with this settlement. I should be sorry indeed to think that he had done otherwise. But to suggest that Colonel Reid Hyde was a necessary instrument in carrying it out is going pretty far. Personally I do not think his presence at Canada House is any help to Canada. It would be a great deal better for Canada if Canada House were turned into an office where Canadians could go and get the information they desired, and where those who are in London seeking information about this dominion might obtain that information in a reasonable and straightforward manner, which is not the case at the present time.

In connection with this
item there is a matter concerning which I wish to make some inquiries, particularly in regard to our minister at Washington. I have reference to the case of a French Canadian widow, Mrs. .Amedee Bilodeau, who has a very large claim against the government of the United States, and which has been in process of settlement-at least, the negotiations have been going on for settlement-for a number of years. The matter has recently been drawn to the attention of the leader of the opposition, and as he was not able to be here ito-day he asked me to bring it up when this vote came before the committee. It is a very grave case of an international character and from the papers I have been able to examine in regard to iit I think this poor woman is suffering a serious injustice at the hands of the United States government. The question is, why our representative in Washington has. not been able to effect some settlement of this woman's claim. The facts, which I shall briefly state, will be in the momory of the Minister of Justice and also of the Solicitor General. They are these:	Amedee Bilodeau of Sherbrooke was shot down in cold blood by an officer of the United States government in Canadian territory on May 29, 1925. The quibble that has taken place during the last three years has been whether it was or was not in Canadian territory; but when one reads the evidence adduced in support of the claim, one is convinced that it is merely a quibble. The unlawful act took place in Canada, and the officer of the American government who perpetrated the offence is at large and has not been prosecuted. This woman has made a plea to the United States government and I think she has enlisted the sympathy of the Department of Justice; considerable correspondence has taken place between the two governments, but the last leter placed in my hands is the reply of the Secretary of State of the United States, expressing the regret of the government of the United States that such a thing should happen, but refusing the claim of the widow for any compensation. This is a matter of international interest; why has not the Department of Justice taken proceedings to arrest the offending officer? If that crime were committed in Canada he could be arrested and extradited, but up to the present time no suoh step has been taken. It was admitted at the outset that the crime did take place in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, that is denied.

I need only take the
statement of the district attorney of Essex county in the state of Vermont, in a letter written on June 18, immediately after the occurrence. As a reason for not prosecuting the offender, who was an official of the United States government, he says:
The case was never presented in our courts because we were satisfied that the shooting of Bilodeau took place in the Dominion of Canada.
There was no prosecution; the man was given his liberty. As I have said, the evidence was submitted to the Department of Justice and was also placed in my hands, and it convinces one that the question of where the actual occurrence took place is merely a quibble. It occurred on the Canadian side of the international boundary, twenty-five or thirty feet in Canada; the man was deliberately shot down by the United States officer, three or four shots being fired at him. He was able to run some three hundred yards before he dropped, and he ran further into Canadian territory. Then he was picked up by the American officer, placed in a motor car and taken to a hospital in the state of Vermont, but was dead before he reached the hospital.
From the record I see that two American officers came to Canada for the purpose of getting evidence with which to break up some illicit drug trading which was being carried on between Canada and the United States. From the evidence one gathers that Bilodeau, the man who was killed, in some way was mixed up with this illegal traffic. These officers were sent to Canada for the purpose of stopping that traffic, if possible. They induced two men in the province of Quebec, Bilodeau the deceased and a man named Price, to get them some narcotic drugs to be taken to the United States. It seems that a certain quantity of drugs was procured in Montreal, and when the parties started to go back to the United States some altercation seems to have arisen when they were at a point in Canada near the international boundary line. What the altercation was I cannot say from the evidence, but it is certain that one of the American officers, who was travelling at the time under an assumed name, deliberately shot down this man Bilodeau. The other American officer drew a revolver and threatened the other man, Price; he severely assaulted him and threatened to shoot him. Bilodeau, however, was illegally shot down in Canadian territory, and I cannot imagine why the Department of Justice has not taken steps to prosecute that man. I fancy they have used the diplomatic

Supply-Representation at Washington
channels in Washington, which not only exist now but which have existed for some time, but there seems to be little or no prospect that they will succeed in getting anything from the government of the United States for this unfortunate woman. The United States apparently allege that there is a great conflict as to whether the act was committed on the Canadian or on the American side of the line; if it was committed on the American side of the line why was not this man prosecuted? If it was committed on the Canadian side of the line why do not our authorities take proceedings now to bring this man to Canada and try him?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend think that if there is a possibility of criminal proceedings, the attorney general) of the province is responsible?
I think the Department of Justice here has been seized of all the facts and has been diligently corresponding with the government of the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was for the purpose of securing compensation for the widow and not in order to institute criminal proceedings.

Unless I am misinformed the Minister of Justice has power to direct the attorney general to lay an information, and I cannot see why this step has not been taken in regard to this case, with which the Department of Justice has greatly concerned itself. Whether or not the door is closed to this woman getting anything in the way of compensation, through the last letter from the Secretary of State for the United States, I do not know, but a glaring wrong has been done in the Dominion of Canada. Our law has been broken, altogether apart from the question of reparation, a crime has been committed in this country by an officer of the American government, and up to the present time no prosecution has taken place. I would ask the Prime Minister to see to it that our representative in Washington, reopens this matter with the authorities of the United States; it is sufficiently serious to be proceeded with. "Let justice be done though the heavens fall" is an old, accepted maxim, but at the present moment we have a condition which permits an official of the United States government to come into Canada and slay a man in cold blood, and no prosecution has yet taken place on either side of the line.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I might say to my hon. friend that this matter is by no means closed. My hon. friend has referred

to a communication from the United States Secretary of State, but the government of Canada does not accept the view of the United States government in, this matter. Within the last week representations on that very point have been made anew to the United States government through our minister at Washington. As my bon. friend has intimated, the United States government hold that the shooting took plane in the United States and that the act was performed in selfdefence. We do not admit that; we contend, as my hon. friend has contended, that the act was committed on this side of the line and that it resulted in the death of an individual whose widow is now entitled to compensation, and we are pressing the claim of the widow in the name of the government of Canada. I can assure my hon. friend that this matter is receiving all the attention which the circumstances will permit at this time.

With regard to this
matter I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether the government will be satisfied with compensation paid to the widow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As the Minister of Justice has just said, with respect to criminal proceedings there is an obligation upon the attorney general of the province; it is not an obligation which rests with the Minister of Justice of the Dominion. As the minister has just reminded me, it is not only an obligation; the power in the matter rests with the province. If the government of Canada succeed in establishing the right of this widow to redress, I assume that of itself will be evidence that a crime has been committed, in which event I would be very much surprised if the province in which it was shown that the act had been committed did not take immediate action.
How is it that it cannot be proven where the crime took place three years ago, and why has the man not been arrested?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are many lawyers interested in the matter and they are leaving nothing undone.
I cannot say much for their efficiency if, after three years, they cannot determine that matter.
I do not think thp lawyers have been exceedingly diligent in having failed to get the proper co-operation from this government.

There is another matter I would like to bring

Supply-Representation at Washington
to the attention of the committee in connection with this Washington embassy. I refer to the question of vessels which have been arrested off the coast of the United States. The case in which I am particularly interested has to do with a vessel owned by a person in my own constituency. This vessel was arrested nineteen miles off the coast of the United States, taken into one of the ports and kept there for eighteen months or two years until the vessel practically went to pieces. The matter was tried in the United States court and it was decided that they had mo business to arrest. This was about three years ago, and from that time the owner has been trying to get redress. I think the matter was before the British minister previous to the appointment of our own minister; then it was handed over to the latter. I have written repeatedly to the department and all I have been able to get so far is the statement that the matter is under consideration. We should, under the treaty, be able to get some action in three years because we have a treaty now between Great Britain and the United States under which such claims can be established and paid. I would ask that some action be taken because I think the matter has been under consideration long enough.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The case my hon. friend has mentioned is similar to a number which have come up within the last year or two, since the treaty to which he refers was signed. Practically al are cases that relate to alleged bootlegging. The government is anxious as far as it is possible to lend no encouragement to this traffic. We have not attempted to press cases where it was not clearly established that a national interest was affected rather than some bootlegging interest. I am afraid the case my hon. friend has in mind has not come clearly in the class of one thaJt is wholly in the national interest. However, I shall! have pleasure in seeing that the matter is looked into further.

I think the department is satisfied about the justice of this claim because it has already been determined by a United States court. There is no question of bootlegging because the vessel was nineteen miles off the coast. The only thing I have to complain of is the delay, because there are special provisions in this treaty whereby all we have to do is to ask for an arbitration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The point, I understand, is largely one of whether the seizure was unreasonable or improper, and any
technical question is perhaps secondary. However, the department will look into the matter further.

Regarding the matter brought up by my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), we could understand a delay in criminal proceedings in Vermont, where they are notoriously slow, as in many of the states of the union, but as a rule we do not find that same lack of desire to prosecute criminal offenders in the provinces of this country. This is a case of great notoriety, and it has been brought to the attention of the Justice department. It has been investigated by them and thaJt department is seized of all the circumstances. I would be glad to know if the Justice department has communicated with the attorney general of the province of Quebec or even with the local crown attorney It is quite conceivable that the matter may not have reached the attention of the authorities in Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am quite sure that
the department of the attorney general in ' Quebec has investigated into the matter. I did not know that this question would come up to-day and I did not look at the papers, but I will be pleased to inquire into the matter.

The Minister of Justice will be aware that if there was neglect in prosecuting, the Department of Justice can hardly keep out of the matter now that they have taken such a prominent part in the whole affair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think the provinces would allow even -the Department of Justice ,at Ottawa to investigate criminal affairs or take their place in regard to these matters.
But they would very readily allow themselves to be pressed by the Minister of Justice to do their duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe the department of the attorney general of Quebec is doing its duty; there has never been any complaint as to that. I think our record in criminal matters in Quebec is clean.

TheTe is no suggestion it is not. Here is a case in which there has been some miscarriage of justice, and the matter is very plainly within the purview of the Justice department here. It seems to me that the Justice department cannot stand aside and let this matter go unchallenged.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the gentleman
interested in this case has made a mistake when he tries to make it a political issue.

I never heard of it before.

There seems to be a
good deal of misunderstanding throughout the country with regard to these passports. For instance, a short time ago a man came to see me who wanted to get a passport to go to the old country. His complaint was that he was informed by the agent of the Canadian National at Edmonton that he woidd have no trouble whatever in Ottawa and he came from Edmonton to this city. He said that if it had not been that parliament was in session and I happened to be in Ottawa, he would have had great difficulty in getting his passport because there was no one else he knew in this city or anywhere east of Alberta to whom he could refer and who could identify him in order that he might

obtain a passport. If we are going to have or if we must have a passport system, the railway agents and others selling tickets and acting as agents for steamship lines ought at least to be compelled to give to those purchasing tickets from them reasonable information regarding passports as well as in respect to all the other things it is necessary for them to know in order to proceed to the full length of the journey on which they are starting.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The same
amount of knowledge with respect to passports is, I believe, current in Canada as in any other country. Anyone going abroad assumes, I imagine, that a passport will be required and it is. very easy for an individual to ascertain where a passport is to be obtained. I think the railway companies, as my hon. friend has suggested, should advise all their agencies fully with respect to that requirement and thus help individuals purchasing tickets readily to obtain the information they need as to passports. I cannot think of any method that could be devised to make it easier for a Canadian citizen to secure a passport than that which exists at the present time.

That is perfectly true
so far as the passport office is concerned, but the railway agents-I think the Minister of Railways might take notice of this, and he might be able to help out-should give correct information and not start people out with wrong information on a journey from the ends of this country to Europe or some other place. The business of the railway agents is to sell tickets and I think they ought at least to be charged with a sense of responsibility and not to give out wrong information to people who are buying tickets from them.

I know as a matter of
fact that all railway agents, particularly in the larger centres, are fully informed regarding the passport requirements, but I would hesitate to assume the responsibility for the possibility of individual error on the part of one or more of the many thousands of station agents in Canada. The railway companies, for the very good commercial reason mentioned by my hon. friend, place their agents in a position to supply a mine of information on many topics and among them is undoubtedly the passport question.

They have forms, I understand.

I have had the same experience. A gentleman who came from my district was told by the agent that it was easy to obtain a passport. He said to him: Go through Ottawa and everything will be lovely. When he arrived in this city no one could identify him. I do not know whether it was the railway agent or a private agent who gave him, as my hon. friend said, false information, failing to tell him that he had to get statements and documents signed by local residents. Had he been told that he would have known what to do. I think some responsibility rests upon the railway companies to instruct their agents to give correct advice. It is a very serious thing for a person to come three thousand miles and then have to go back or wait here for some weeks in order to get the necessary documents.
I will see that this discussion is communicated to both railway companies.

Could the Prime Minister on this item assist me in a difficulty that has arisen in my constituency? An Italian named Gesmina, residing in Guelph, a British subject, who was not familiar with the passport regulations, went to Italy last August taking with him his naturalization certificate instead of a passport. He landed in Italy and although now he desires to return to Canada they will not let him out of Italy. The Italian government take the position that he entered Italy without a passport and he must not leave the country. I cannot get a passport for him now because I have no photograph of him. They think if Canadians have passports they will be subjected to less in the way of questioning.

I am only surprised there is so little trouble. If it were not that we have a particularly efficient and courteous staff in connection with the passport office, we would have a great deal more trouble. I have another matter to bring to the notice of the Prime Minister. Complaints have been received by the leader of the opposition and no doubt by the Prime Minister himself from various cities in Canada where there is a more or less extensive Jewish population, asking that something be done in regard to the alleged persecution of the Jewish people in Roumania and, I think, in other eastern European states. The writers of these letters inquire why something cannot be done by Canada's representative on the League of Nations. I would ask the Prime Minister if this matter has been brought to his attention and if any steps have been taken to mitigate the trouble in regard to the Jewish population particularly in Roumania. I understand that anti-Jewish agitations have been going on in that country for some time. I he relatives of many of these people are residents of the Dominion of Canada and they are naturally much alarmed at conditions which exist in Roumania. They expect, I think very reasonably, that our representative on the League of Nations should take this matter up with the idea of having these persecutions stopped.

As my hon. friend knows, Canada is represented on the council of the league, and I am sure that the circumstance will occasion an extra interest on Canada's part in the matter which my hon. friend has brought up.

There is one other matter pertaining to the League of Nations. Complaints have also been -made, and I have no doubt to the government as well as to the leader of the opposition, in regard to German currency which is held in this country to a considerable extent and was purchased during or after the war. It is said that in some countries German currency has already been redeemed out of the alien enemy property which has accumulated in the hands of receivers in various countries. Could the matter be taken up either at the League of Nations or in any other quarter to see if some compensation could not be made to the holders of this German currency? Canada obtains a large amount of reparation -money. Is there any provision in regard to that reparation money for the redeeming of this German currency?

subsubtopic: LONDON AND PORT BURWELL RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
This is a bill to incorporate the London and Port Burwell Railway Company. The company propose to construct and operate a railroad line from the town of Port Burwell, in the county of Elgin, in the province of Ontario, to the city of London, in the county of Middlesex, in the province of Ontario, a distance of some thirty-four miles. At Port Burwell, the lake terminal of this railway, there is a well-developed harbour capable of accommodating the largest lake vessels. This harbour has a channel depth of about 25 feet and a turning basin of 650 feet. Only one side of this harbour is being utilized at the present time, yet it

London and Port Burwell Railway
contributed last year over $160,000 to the revenue of this Dominion. The inland terminal of this railway line will be the city of London, with a population of approximately 65,000 people. London is recognized as a distributing point for freight in southwestern Ontario.
The primary object in constructing this railway is to supply cheap transportation facilities for the products of coking ovens, which this company propose to build at Port Burwell. This is provided for in the amendment as clause 16, which reads as follows:
Provided, however, the Board of Railway Commissioners shall not exercise its powers under sections 106, 167 and 170 of the Railway Act except and until either:-
(a)	a coking plant, fully equipped, has been established at or near Port Burwell at a cost of at least $700,000; or
(b)	a bona fide contract has been' entered between responsible parties for the construction of a coking plant, fully equipped, to be established at or near Port Burwell at a cost of, at least, $700,000 and a sum of, at least, $200,000 has been expended in and/or on the construction of such coking plant; all to the satisfaction of the Board of Railway Commissioners.
' Western Ontario will thus be assured of an industrial development of the greatest value to that section of the province, helping to solve the fuel problem in that locality and also assist in the establishmenet of other industries which are sure to follow -a development of this kind.
This bill was gone into very thoroughly in the committee and it was shown that the freight to be carried by this company will be new business, a product of their own development. I feel that I scarcely need appeal to the house for the passing of this bill when hon. members become aware that favourable action will mean the expenditure or employment of a large amount of new capital in the country, and capital which will assist in solving a great problem in the industrial and economic life of Ontario. In doing this it will not place any burden whatever upon any part of our country.
I should like to emphasize one more point, Mr. Chairman, and that is that the promoters of this company are not asking, nor do they intend to ask, for any assistance, financially or otherwise, except that they be given the privilege to spend their money in this manner. When the question of the capital necessary for the construction of this project was discussed in the committee, clause (4), providing for the capital stock of the company, was deleted from the bill. I, therefore, beg to move:
That the following be inserted in the said bill as clause 4:-
The capital stock of the company shall be five hundred thousand dollars.
