subsubtopic: LONDON AND PORT BURWELL RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Before this clause is declared carried I wish to make a few remarks in regard to this bill. I represent the city of London in this house, that city being the northern terminus of the proposed line, and I am opposed to the passing of the bill. I think I can give the committee some good reasons why the bill should not be passed.
This bill proposes to grant a charter to a railroad from Port Burwell to London, Port Burwell being on the north shore of lake Erie. There is already a railroad in operation running from the shore of lake Erie to London, and owned very largely by the city of London-the London and Port Stanley Railway. The proposed line starts at Port Burwell, which is about seventeen or eighteen miles east of Port Stanley, and runs to London in a northwesterly direction. The route of the London and Port Stanley road, which connects London with Port Stanley, is a direct line south by the shortest possible route to the shore of the lake. This road is about twenty-four miles long, while the proposed London and Port Burwell road would be thirty-four miles long, according to the sponsor of the bill.
I should like to give the committee a short history of the existing road. In the early days before railroad accommodation was what it is to-day, London suffered a great deal from very high freight rates, and in an endeavour to extricate herself from that position-and in fact the people of St. Thomas were in the same position-certain residents and officials of London and also of St. Thomas organized a company and secured a charter for the London and Port Stanley Railway. That charter was secured in 1853 so that the road has been in existence for seventy-five years. When the charter was secured there were a few private shareholders concerned as well as the municipalities of London and St. Thomas. The road commenced operations under the direction of the London and Port Stanley Railway Company in 1856 and it continued under that direction until 1874. It was then rented to the Great Western Railway and that lease ran for twenty years. The Great

London and Port Burwell Railway
Western Railway was absorbed in 1882, the Grand Trunk Railway took over that road and also of course took over the lease of the London and Port Stanley Railway. The Grand Trunk railway operated the latter road until 1892 and then, having failed to secure the stock of the road by purchase at its own price, it abandoned operations in 1892, two years before the expiration of the lease. During this time the Grand Trunk secured some shares of the stock and the stock now stands about four-fifths owned by the city of London and one-fifth owned by the Grand Trunk or the Canadian National Railways.
London bought out the shares of the city of St. Thomas in 1893, paying therefor the sum of 840,000. After the cessation of operations by the Grand Trunk there was a period in which a certain United States syndicate rented the road, but they did not operate it very long. They gave it up and finally the city of London leased it to the Pere Marquette Railway for a period of twenty-one years for a rental of about $12,000 per annum. The operation by steam continued until 1915, but it was not very satisfactory and the roadbed and bridges were allowed to depreciate. The service as regards both passenger and freight were very poor. In fact business declined very materially and of course the trunk roads had no particular object in keeping the road open to the lake. The longer haul west or east gave a great deal more to those railroads than they could get by bringing material from Port Stanley to London; so the road was allowed to decline. Prior to 1914 the city of London had invested about $520,000. That was an actual investment of cash and there were certain arrears of interest which amounted to a great deal more than that. In 1914 the city of London, being the largest creditor, took over the road. It rebuilt it, installed new 80-pound rails, new bridges, new stations and freight houses, new carshops and barns, and a great deal of new rolling stock was purchased. The road was electrified and London started operations in 1914, using hydro-electric current as the motive power.
I should like to say a word about the construction of the line. Some people have the idea that an electric line is some little line that runs alongside a highway without any particular regard for curves, grades or anything of that kind and that it probably runs all over the countryside before reaching its destination. But in this case it is a line that goes straight from London to the lake and the rails which weTe put in by the city of London

in 1914 are 80-pound rails. A great deal of broken stone was used as ballast and the other construction pertaining to electrical matters is also up to date. The road was electrified largely by the enterprise of the late Sir Adam Beck, and in installing that equipment he had the idea of making the road a standard for the hydro-radials which he was then promoting. Consequently the construction is particularly good. For example, the method of suspending the live wire is a little out of the ordinary. Steel towers were used set in cement instead of the ordinary wooden poles, and cables were stretched from tower to tower with a certain amount of sag between towers. The live wire was suspended from the cable by hangers of varying lengths in such a way that the live wire is horizontal throughout its length.
I am giving these details so that the committee will understand just how important this installation is and how well it was done. In fact the character of the construction is comparable with that which is used in electric tracks through tunnels and also in United^ States cities where they do not allow steam locomotives to go into the centre of the city. The construction is first class throughout and is such that steam roads have been using that electric road on occasions when they have mishaps on their own lines. Only three weeks ago I saw several freight trains come in hauled by Wabash engines which came over from St. Thomas to London and thence went east on the Canadian National. In that construction the city of London spent from 1914 to 1927 some $1,434,000. The road is of great importance to the whole district and particularly to London where there are three large industrial establishments situated along the line. One of these is the stove and furnace branch of the McClary works, advertised as being the largest stove and furnace plant under the British flag. Thus hon. members can see that the Port Stanley road is of great importance to the city of London in regard to freight handling. It also provides an entrance to the city of London from the city of St. Thomas by the Michigan Central, that road having made an arrangement with the London and Port Stanley for the handling of freight. That arrangement is subject to revision every five years and subject also to the approval of the Dominion railway commission.
At Port Stanley the harbour has been greatly improved by the Dominion public works department. We have twenty-two feet of water in the inner harbour and twenty-

London and Port Burwell Railway
four feet outside with about one thousand feet of dockage and a turning basin probably eight or nine hundred feet in diameter. A great deal of freight is brought in by boat to Port Stanley. The Cleveland and Canada Navigation Company run passenger and package freight boats from Cleveland. The Canada Steamship Company make Port Stanley a port of call and a great deal of package freight is handled from Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, up to Port Stanley and consequently through western Ontario by the London and Port Stanley road. Then we have a car ferry which connects Conneaut with Port Stanley and which handles about 35 or 40 loaded cars per trip. We also have the Century Coal Company which is established there, handling coal in bulk. It proposes to handle about 300,000 tons of coal this year. In committee the statement was made that the London and Port Stanley railwaj'' could not handle coal. The fact is that the London and Port Stanley railway has been handling coal every day, and has done so for twenty years or more. I have a communication here from the manager of the road in regard to its capacity as a freight-handling proposition, from which I should like to quote a few paragraphs. He says:
We have three sixty-ton electric locomotives, each equipped with four 250-horsepower motors.
The statement was made in committee that eight hundred tons of freight was the limit of a train load. I explained to the committee that while 800 tons is the limit handled to-day, it is not necessarily the limit that can be handled by these locomotives. That figure of eight hundred tons is set in order to keep the power charges down. Those who understand the method of charging for electric current will very readily understand that the peak load charge in connection with electric energy is a very heavy one. The charges for electric energy are computed in two ways: First, in computing the monthly power bill there is tihe demand or peak load charge, which is based on the highest horse-power used for a period of ten minutes during any day during the month in which the power is delivered. After that, the charge for the current is so much per kilowatt hour. Inasmuch as the charge for peak load or demand makes up about one-third to one-half of the power bill, it will be readily understood that it is very important to keep down the peak load. The manager says:
Eight hundred tons of coal is the maximum tonnage allowed for one train for the purpose 56103-223
of keeping the power peak down, but this is not the capacity haul of one locomotive. One locomotive could haul from Port Stanley to St. Thomas approximately 1,040 tons. If volume of business warranted and power was available, then it no doubt would be profitable to raise the tonnage allowance to the limit.
Further he says, referring to a vessel load of coal which came in shortly before he wrote:
With reference to the movement of 7,000 tons of coal which arrived at Port Stanley in one vessel, it will be noted that a total of 120 cars, comprising 7,200 tons, was handled from Port Stanley and delivered to our connections within the time of 50 hours. Other business handled northbound for the same period consisted of 1,731 tons, which comprised car ferry business and regular business between St. Thomas and London. Southbound movements during the same time accounted for 4,493 tons.
He also says, in regard to capacity:
The maximum number of tons that could be handled by one sixty-ton locomotive with the present restriction of 800 tons out of Port Stanley would be approximately 9,360 tons per day. The maximum number of tons that could be handled with one sixty-ton locomotive with no power restrictions would be approximately 12,480 tons per day.
So the committee can very readily see that the question of insufficient power or insufficient equipment is not a vital one, because the road is well equipped in those respects, and can handle all the tonnage that is available.
Then in addition to the freight business, the passenger business has developed to a great extent. Port Stanley has become a very popular summer resort, as it has a very desirable bathing beach and picnic ground. Since electrification there has been a marked increase in passenger traffic. The passenger business in the last year of steam operation (1915), amounted to 100,000 paying passengers. In both 1925 and 1926 there were over 1,000,000 paid passages each year on the railway, and last year, 1927, there were 700,000 passengers carried.
Now a word as to the management and the general financial results. First of all, I want to explain to the committee just how this road is being operated by the city of London. The London and Port Stanley Railway Company as at first organized is still in existence. That company is comprised of the mayor of the city of London as president, and eight aldermen, composing the board of directors, the city clerk acting as secretary. The company thus organized took over the property in 1914, and leased it from January 1, 1914, to the'city of London for a period of ninety-nine years. The city of London appoints the London railway commission, which operates

3522	COMMONS
London and Port Burwell Railway
the road. That lease and that agreement were confirmed by an act of this parliament, chapter 16 of the statutes of Canada, 1914. By it, certain rentals are payable to the city of London varying from $20,000 per year up until 1923, to larger amounts, until $50,000 per year is reached in the final years of the lease.
As to the financial outcome of our operations, the road from 1916 to 1921 paid all expenses, all taxes, rentals, operating costs, interest and sinking fund and had a surplus each year of quite a substantial sum. About that time, owing to the establishment of good roads, the competition of motor trucks and passenger automobiles became so severe that the surpluses were changed to deficits, and since then we have had a deficit each year. I should like to quote from the manager's statement in the year 1925. He says that between July 1, 1915, and December 31, 1923, the railroads paid to the city of London in rentals, $170,000; sinking fund, $170,600; accumulated surpluses, $157,000; and some other items which are too small to enumerate, which make a total of about $527,000 or a yearly average of $62,000. Those are profits over and above operating charges, interest on debentures, taxation, and other items that are met out of earning. This road is of such importance to the city of London that even if a loss were incurred each year, I am very much of the opinion that London would continue to operate the road and consider it good business, not only because of the freight that is handled, but because of the means it affords of getting people to Port Stanley.
The early stages of the road's operation proved that the road can be operated at a profit provided sufficient business is available. The difficulty is .that the road is in more or less of a starved condition so far as traffic is concerned, but physically it is kept up in A-l condition. The position is this: We need more business, and the statement of the manager of the road is that it could handle three times the business it now handles if the traffic were available. In that case, of course, the overhead would be spread over a larger tonnage, and consequently it would be much easier to make the road pay.
This is not the first time that competition has been offered to the London and Port Stanley railway. The Southwestern Traction Company started in business in 1906 or 1907. It inaugurated a line from London, through Lambeth to Port Stanley, and did a considerable business in its early years, but it failed to make profits, and was taken Over in 1910 by the London and Lake Erie Transportation Company. That company had

charters for building roads to various towns and villages in western Ontario-Port Burwell, by the way, was one of them-but after operating about five years it was forced into liquidation, and those who had invested their money in it, including many farmers and others residing along the line of the road, lost large sums. This is proof of the fact that there is not enough business in that section of the country to keep two roads operating at a profit.
There was another line which proposed to come into competition with the London and Port Stanley railway, and that was the Erie, London and Tillsonburg railway. A charter was granted for that railway in 1906, and although five or six extensions of time were granted, no work was done and the charter finally expired in 1916, those who had taken out the charter evidently not being convinced that there was a prospect of sufficient business even to start operations.
The proposed charter is opposed by the London railway commission. In a resolution, after reciting the circumstances, they state:
It is the wish of the commission that the council write the member for the city of London and ask him to do everything possible to oppose the granting of a charter to the London and Port Burwell Railway Company.
The London chamber of commerce are also on record in the following resolution:
This civic institution therefore supports the London and Port Stanley railway commission of the city of London in the protest agains-* the granting of the charter to the proposed Port Burwell-London Railway and desires to register this decision with the member for London.
The city council of London are also on record in the same direction in the following resolution:
Be it therefore resolved that the federal government be petitioned to refuse the application, and the clerk instructed to furnish every member of the federal parliament with a copy of this resolution, and the member for London and the several members of the federal parliament urged to oppose the granting of the said application.
Then it is opposed by the city council of St. Thomas in a resolution which reads as follows:
That Mr. M. F. Hepburn, M.P., be advised that the St. Thomas city council are opposed to the proposed London and Port Burwell Railway Company as set forth in the application dated at Tillsonburg January 26, 1928, a copy of which was sent to this council by Donald F. Gibson, solicitor for the applicants.

speechtext:
Is not the hon. member well aware of the fact that since that time the city council have passed a second resolution in which they state that the city of

London and Port Burwell Railway
St. Thomas is content to leave the matter of the London and Port Burwell Railway charter to my judgment?

subsubtopic: LONDON AND PORT BURWELL RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I was not aware of that fact. I did hear a statement made by the member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) that the mayor of St. Thomas had sent him a telegram in which he said something of the kind; but it was a private telegram, and inasmuch as the horn, member did not quote any communication from himself to the mayor, it is pretty hard to tell what circumstances brought about that message. But this resolution is dated May 3, and so far as I know is the last official record on the books of the city council of St. Thomas. It might be of interest too to the hon. member for West Elgin to look up some of the press notices in which it is stated that the people of Port Burwell will boycott the people of London and St. Thomas because of their objection to the London and Poi't Burwell Railway charter. So while the mayor of St. Thomas and the hon. member are in agreement, there are probably other people in St. Thomas who will have something to say about that a little later on. This application is also opposed by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways. I shall have something to say about the railway situation a little later.
According to clause 16 of the bill, it ia proposed to install a coking plant at Port Burwell with a daily capacity of 675 tons. We contend that such a coking plant might very well be located at Port Stanfcy, for the reason that it would put the producers of coke in closer proximity to St. Thomas and London, and I have no doubt an arrangement might be arrived at with the London railway commission whereby the gias, a by-product of the coking process, could be piped to those two cities along the right of way of the London and Port Stanley railway. The London and Port Stanley railway is well able to handle all the coke that may be turned out by the proposed plant at rates fixed, of course, by the Dominion railway commission. The London railway commission is ready to talk business with the promoters of the coking plant and we contend that a daily output of 675 tons is not sufficient to warrant the building of another railway line.
I oppose the bill for the reasons that I have enumerated, and also on account of the increased losses which will be incurred by the city of London if the proposed railway is built. The city of London has invested roughly about two million dollars in cash in
the London and Port Stanley railway, and any division of the existing business must of course result in further loss to the city.
I contend, Mr. Chairman, that there is no demand for increased railway facilities in the district to be traversed by the projected line. It is already served by the Canadian Pacific railway running from Port Burwell to Inger-soll and thence to London, Port Burwell being served by this railway and Port Stanley by the London and Port Stanley railway. The proposed line starting from London will cross the Canadian Pacific railway running from St. Thomas to Ingersoll; it will cross the doubletrack line of the Michigan Central railway, running from St. Thomas to the Niagara district; it will also cross the Canadian National railway at Aylmer, making these three crossings in a distance of less than ten miles. The district is well served with railways. There is no influx of population, there is no increase in manufacturing, there are no new industries to any marked extent, and from a very careful scaling of the map I find that no section of the district is more than eight or nine miles from a railway; in fact I am quite within the mark when I say that ninety per cent of the people live closer than five miles to a railway. I repeat, the district is well served with railways and does not need any more trackage.
The sponsor of the bill stated that this coking freight would be all new business, but, as I have stated, there is no influx of population, and consequently no increased demand for fuel and things of that kind. The present business will have to be divided among all the roads already operating there, and if one more is built it means that there will be so much less business for each road. May I have the attention of the Minister of Railways for a moment?

speechtext: Certainly.

speechtext:

The hon. member has

Certain statements have been made with regard to the attitude of the people of the city of St. Thomas, and as the representative of that city I feel it my duty to spend a few minutes explaining the situation. The people of that locality realize that new developments have taken place in the transportation of coal into southern Ontario. Instead of taking it by freight around the lake they are now inaugurating cross-lake shipment in bulk. They must therefore provide proper facilities. This new company first approached the London and

Port Stanley Railway with a view to buying the road but it was not for sale. Then they turned to Port Burwell harbour, where the government has spent $1,500,000. They bought a piece of land there on the assurance that there would be no opposition from the city of London. They then propose to build from Burwell to London a line which does not parallel the London and Port Stanley railway.
The present objection coming from the London and Port Stanley railway is hard to understand especially in view of the fact, not only that they are in financial difficulties today, but that the crown attorney of the county of Middlesex is investigating charges of corruption and bribery against the London and Port Stanley Railway. In fact, the mayor of London was elected on an issue which involved the operations of the London and Port Stanley Railway. That railway is claimed to be a political enterprise. As a matter of fact there is very little sympathy for that railway and its present management.
In regard to the opposition of St. Thomas, it is true that they passed a resolution opposing the railway unless it came through the city of St. Thomas. At the same time the city of London was opposing the same railway on the ground that it was proposed to build the railway to the city of London. This only shows the anomaly of the situation. Later on the city council of St. Thomas passed a resolution to the effect that they were content to leave to my judgment the matter of the railway charter, and that is the present position so far as St. Thomas is concerned.
I have here several letters, one in particular from the reeve of the township of Yarmouth, in that locality, who states that after making a careful investigation with regard to the proposed line he finds that the people of that district are very much in sympathy with the new railway, and that no doubt it will be connected with one of the biggest industrial developments now pending in southern Ontario. As a guarantee of good faith in the matter, these people are willing to build an $800,000 coking plant and to spend several millions in the construction of their railway. They have made a careful survey of the whole situation and have definite plans establishing the feasibility of the project. I will not take up the time of the committee further, and in view of the fact that we have only a few minutes left for the consideration of private bills, I move that this bill be reported.	.

As this is a vote in respect of the Department of National Revenue, perhaps I may be allowed a few moments to call attention to the fa)ct that the customs and excise enforcement officer at Notre Dame des Bois was dismissed for partisanship. In the reply to an inquiry which I made of the minister I find that this officer, who was dismissed on December 6, 1926, had been for seven years and seven months an efficient officer of that department, and that during that time he had paid 5 per cent of his salary as a contribution to the superannuation fund.
Supply-National Revenue

No inquiry was granted; in his reply the minister stated that an inquiry was asked for by the service bureau of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League and I am informed, although I have not the documents here, that this official also asked for an inquiry. Whatever may happen in regard to the Post Office department, I say that an officer who has served for seven years, who has paid several hundreds of dollars into the superannuation fund, and has been an efficient officer without any complaint being made against him during that term of years, should not be dismissed without an inquiry, on the word of any member of parliament or any supporter of the government.
If I am not mistaken,, the alleged political partisanship of this officer-I 'trust I am not confusing him with another dismissal, but unfortunately I have not the documents of the file in my desk to-night-took place when he was not at the office at Notre Dame des Bois, but when he was absent performing a special duty at the bolder. I am informed that the office of the customs department at Notre Dame des Bois is in a building which is used in part for the customs office, another part being rented for other offices, and the upper portion of the building being used as a residence. During the election campaign when this officer was absent, not in town at all but miles and miles away, the proprietor of this building allowed the Conservative candidate, who had his campaign quarters in a (building on the opposite side of the street, to stretch a line on which hie put a flag indicating to the passers-by on the street where the Conservative headquarters were. I am informed that this official had absolutely nothing to do with that. As I said, he was away on special service at the border, and if the facts as reported to me are correct an inquiry should certainly be granted, and I am surprised that none was granted.
He was dismissed on the complaint of partisanship made by a member of parliament. If the government are going to dismiss officials of long standing, with competent and efficient service, without an inquiry when asked for, they at least should have the sense of justice to hand back their contributions to the superannuation fund. I think the matter is one that should be inquired into carefully, and I trust that the minister, despite the fact that, he has taken action on the word of a member, will! inquire further. I am not imputing any dishonesty to the member, but I know that in my own constituency I have often received information by word of mouth which I found to be utterly unreliable. There should be some ways and means of getting

behind mere gossip and inquiring into the facts to ascertain whether this man has really been a political partisan during the election.
For my own part, I entirely disagree with the practice that has been followed by both political parties with regard to dismissals for partisanship. I have felt that way ever since I wias a young man in Nova Scotia. I went to address a political meeting in Tusket, Yarmouth county, and my mother was lying ill at the village where I was born, some four or five miles out. I wenit to see her and had dinner with her, and when I got off the train, it being a small village, I had difficulty in finding someone to drive me across country. I asked a relative of mine, who happened to be the village postmaster, to drive me to the place where I was to meet Sir Charles Tupper and address the meeting, and the result was that that relative was dismissed because he had done me the kindness to drive me across country from my mother's place to the village of Tusket. As a young man, the thing rankled in my mind for many years, and ever since I have been opposed to dismissals of that class for so-called political partisanship.

I will admit that the matter
to which the hon. member has just referred has given me some little concern. The dismissal took place entirely in accordance with the principle that has been observed by all parties. The complaint of a member of the house that an individual has been exercising partisanship in elections has always been accented by the minister as a reason for dismissal. I have followed that principle, but I am glad to say there have not been many instances in my own department. I am not going to express an opinion as to whether that is a good practice to follow, although perhaps I might be just so bold as to say that I have a good deal of sympathy with the position 'taken by my hon. friend. Although many members may differ with me, I can see no particular reason why, where a man happens to be in the service of the government, he should not be allowed to exercise any influence he may have on behalf of any political principle in which he believes. However, I will have to take any responsibility there may be in following out the .practice that has always been followed.
So far as the complaint of the man is concerned, I do not recall that he himself made an application for an investigation. So far as my memory serves me, an application for an investigation did come from some soldiers' organization. A reply was sent to the effect that an inquiry would be granted, but I under-

Supply-National Revenue
stand that no further application was made, and that the man disappeared entirely from the neighbourhood in which he had been employed.
I am informed that he had to go to another district to earn a living for himself and some others who were dependent on him.

If the man has returned and desires an investigation I shall certainly comply with his wishes. I will be quite frank and say that once an officer has been discharged in accordance with this particular custom-I am referring to the word of a member-if it is found that he has not been guilty of such practices, I do not know just how he could be restored. The Civil Service Commission, of course, would have to reappoint him.
Supposing it were found on investigation that the man was a Liberal, what would you do then?

I will say very frankly, to
my hon. friend, and I think he will believe me, that it would not make any difference. The Civil Service Commission is the body entirely in control of that matter.
Another point was mentioned in regard to this matter-the return to ithe discharged employee of the sum which he had paid into the fund. Personally, I am of the opinion- I am not speaking for the government-that no matter what the reason might be for discharging an employee, he is entitled to receive back the actual amount of money he has paid into the treasury.

Surely it would
be a comparatively simple matter to reimburse a man the amount he has paid in, and surely a man is not to be turned out without even the semblance of a trial. That, I understand, is what the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) is contending. If this house is to accept as a guiding rule in the future that the government is going to act upon the basis of turning men out without an investigation to get the particulars, let us know it, and let us be guided by it, but let the position be definite.

I would say to my hon.
friend that it has been very definite in the past, as the member for S't. Lawrence-St. George stated a moment ago, and the practice that was followed in this case has been the practice for many years under all governments. If the practice is wrong and the house decides so, it might be well to change it.

That is what I
am asking the minister. It being wrong, let us change it.

I agree entirely with the
hon. member for West Hamilton and with the remarks made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. The fact that a rule of this kind was established by a Tory government does not mean that it is right. I believe in following the Tory party when they are right but certainly not when they are wrong. This seems to be a flagrant case of injustice in dismissing a man from his employment on the mere statement of a member of parliament. Sometimes even members of parliament make mistakes. After all I do not consider that the word of a member of parliament is to be looked upon as Holy Writ. This case is unusual and it seems to me1 that it behooves the Liberal party, which always claims to be a little better than the other parties, to change the rule and to see that justice is done to this man, be he Liberal or Conservative or even Progressive. My good friend the Minister of National Revenue is not bound by rules which he found in the department when he came in, whether they were laid down by Liberals or by Conservatives. He is a man of pretty independent views and I am surprised that, having a case of this kind before him, he would be willing to follow in the footsteps of former ministers who were not quite so punctilious as he is in matters of this kind. If this rule was wrong, I do not care whether it was inaugurated by Liberals or by Conservatives, surely we ought to have manliness and independence enough to set it right. An investigation ought to be had into the case and if the facts are as stated by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, the man ought to be reinstated.

I should like to ask the
minister whether under the regime of this government, if not under himself, it has not been the practice to take the word of a defeated candidate and to have a man dismissed without investigation. I am not at all sure about the matter and I am asking for information only.

I can speak only for myself. It has never been done so far as I am concerned. The word of a defeated candidate or anyone else is not taken, but a commissioner may be appointed who makes an investigation and upon his report an official may be dismissed. So far as I know a dismissal never takes place except on the word

of the sitting member. I presume the theory of taking his word is that an hon. member is responsible to the house for his actions.
Is the defeated candidate's word not taken just as readily as that of the sitting member?
No.
It has been done regularly in post office positions in my district.

It has been in the Post
Office department in my constituency in a number of cases. It was done in the case of a candidate who was defeated three times in my constituency. He ran four elections and won one, and his word is taken as gospel in regard to positions in the Post Office department. I do not know about the Department of National Revenue. While I am on my feet I should like to ask the minister why the recommendation from the Civil Service Commission for an appointment to the Digby customs house a year ago this month was not accepted. The minister will remember that we had a conversation last year with reference to an assistant in the Digby customs house and he stated to me that an appointment would be made, but that it would have to come through the Civil Service Commission and that he would ask the Civil Service Commission to ask for candidates. A competition was held in Digby a year ago this month and eight competitors wrote the examination. Three of them passed the examination and the one who passed with the highest marks was a returned soldier. He was recommended by the Civil Service Commission for the appointment, but he was turned down; no appointment was made and the collector has had to do his own work there for the past year and a half, being overworked all the time. This spring, only a few weeks ago, an assistant from the Halifax customs house was sent to Digby, while a local man, a returned soldier, was turned down. I should like to have the minister's explanation.

The explanation is very
simple. Very serious charges were made against the first two of those who had passed the examination. An investigation is being held and in the meantime a relieving officer is being placed in the port.

The young man who was
turned down was afterwards employed by the Dominon Atlantic Railway as an employee in their station at Digby and he is serving the public there. This is a private corpora-

tion. There is absolutely nothing against his character or his ability. He is well qualified for the position and he was so recommended by the Civil Service Commission; but I can tell you why he was not appointed. The defeated candidate in Digby-Annapolis was the man who said that he should not be appointed. That is the whole and sole reason. It is all very well for the Minister of National Revenue to say that his department is free from politics, but in my constituency they have been playing politics in regard to every appointment that has been made.

If the investigation shows
that there is no ground for the complaint, the Civil Service Commission, so far as I am concerned, will be allowed to go on and make the appointment.
It will not be a non-partisan investigation that will take place.
That is a point that ought to be cleared up. Who is to be the investigator and who raised the charges against this returned soldier? What are the facts?

It is not going to be a
partisan investigation at all. The investigation will be made by officers of the department, not by any partisan commissioner.

Why has the minister taken a whole year to look into the matter? He has known for more than a year that the collector of customs at my port has been overworked. He has had no assistance whatever since his appointment some two years ago, while other officers that have no more business, and indeed not as much business to deal with as there is at my port, have two or three assistants. This man was not appointed simply because he was not satisfactory to the defeated candidate in the constituency. That is the whole reason. There is nothing against his character or ability. He is qualified in every particular for the position.

I have been greatly interested in some of the discussion to-night. Personally I have never been in favour of the principle of dismissing men for partisan reasons. Had I taken that position I could certainly have had a number of men dismissed following the election of 1921. In that respect I have differed with many of my friends at home, men who have voted for me. They say that the Liberals do not take as good care of their friends as the Conservatives do. When I went home at Easter I had some criticisms made of myself just on that score.

Supply-National Revenue
la communications that I have had with the Minister of National Revenue in relation to some complaints that have been made, reasons were urged why certain officials should be dismissed. I may say that the Minister of National Revenue was very careful about the investigations he made and he did not show any willingness to dismiss men without cause.
I am glad to hear these protestations of high principle coming from the opposite side and I hope they will be followed in the future. Certainly I know the condition of things in the past, particularly in regard to the election of 1911, were different because the Conservative candidate during that election campaign carried around in his pocket dismissals and appointments. The practice then was very different from the principle which has now been proclaimed as the proper one to follow. Personally, I agree absolutely with the principle that has been enunciated that men should not be dismissed simply because they have seen fit to exercise their privileges as citizens. I hold to that, and I have held to it both in opposition and when I was supporting the government of the day.
Mr' MANION: When was the hon. member in opposition?

That is not the question at the present time. I have been in opposition to governments of the day, and I have supported governments of the day, just as the hon. member has, and I have always advocated that principle, thereby bringing upon myself the displeasure of some of my friends who took the ground that the Liberals had not taken as good care of their friends as the Conservatives had done in the past. I hope the protest that has been made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George will have some weight, and that the principles which he has enunciated will be applied impartially by all parties in this house, and by this as well as and by successive governments.
In connection with the case mentioned by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, is the minister going to make the investigation asked for, or is he not?

I have answered that. If
a man makes an application to have an investigation, he will certainly have it.

What is the minister going
to do about this case? He must certainly remember the conversation we had last year,
in which he stated that he would ask the Civil Service Commission to hold examinations, and that he would ha.ve a local man appointed. The examinations were held, and the one that passed the highest-and only three out of the eight passed- was a returned soldier, who was well qualified in every respect for the position. The Civil Service Commission recommended his appointment, but he has never been appointed, and an outside man has been sent there instead. The people of Digby resent that, because we have hundreds of well qualified people capable of filling the position. I want to know what the minister is going to do in connection with that position.

I am not sure that I can
add anything to what I have said. Complaints did come-
From whom?

If the hon. gentleman will
permit me, I will answer him. Complaints were made, and they were of a serious nature. If they are true, whether the Civil Service Commission recommends that man or not, he will not be accepted by this department. If they are not true, and the investigation is going to be made by men who are not partisan, then the commission may make the appointment, and I shall not interfere.
Just one other word. The man who has been sent there has not been sent there as a permanent official at all, but merely as a temporary official to take the office until a permanent appointment can be made.

I have known this young
man for twenty years, and there is absolutely nothing against his character. I have never heard a word against him, unless the fact that he may have voted for me is against him. If that is going to be the excuse for keeping him out of the position to which he is entitled, it is time this house knew it.
Would the minister be good enough to inform the committee when these complaints were made, and by whom?
I have not the data here.

Approximately,
how long is it since they were made?

I think they came in some
months ago, speaking from memory-last fall, the commissioner tells me.

Then, why has not the investigation taken place long before this?	.
The place was not filled because during the winter the officer was not required.
But why was not the investigation of these complaints held sooner?
It is being held now.
Why is it being held now, and not months ago?
We have lots of work to do.

I am not going to enter into a discussion regarding the dismissal of officials. I was amazed at the statement of the minister that his predecessors had dismissed officers on the recommendation of the members. I know that that is not true so far as the Conservatives are concerned.
I said nothing about my predecessors at all.
The minister said that that was the habit and custom of the ministers holding portfolios in the government.
I was speaking of all governments, not of my predecessors in this particular office. I made no reference to them whatever.

Well, predecessors in other departments. I for one object to allowing that statement to go unchallenged. I know it is not correct. I know Conservative ministers who were asked to dismiss men on the Liberal side because of their interference in politics in my riding, and the government of the day refused to dismiss them, and in some cases I think they were right. But I did not rise to discuss that feature at all. I rose to say one word in support of a remark that was made by the minister. He claimed that there is something wrong and something unjust in allowing a civil servant to contribute to a fund for a number of years, and then to be dismissed and receive no refund of his contribution or any part of it. I have in mind the case of a man who had paid into this fund for fifteen years, and was dismissed a year or so ago. I am not going to complain because he was dismissed; I am not going to discuss that at all. He committed an offence which most men would regard as a pardonable offence, and this government dismissed him. My point is that having paid into the fund for fifteen years he applied to have his contributions returned. It took one year to get the government to agree to make this refund

of his contributions. Probably they had some justification for the delay; I am not going to discuss that point, but in refunding his contributions nothing was allowed by way of interest on what he had paid in. I think that is wrong. I claim that that provision in the act should be amended, and I hope the minister will bring in an amendment next session to provide that no matter what a man may be dismissed for, if he has contributed for a number of years to the superannuation fund he shall get his money back. The minister himself spoke somewhat to that effect, and not much attention was paid to it. I consider that it was a very important declaration, and I desire to commend the minister for it, and I hope that he will carry out that idea. There is something absolutely wrong in deducting five per cent of a man's wages for five, ten or fifteen years, and then dismissing him for some simple offence and not refund to Ihim, what he has paid in. I trust that an amendment will be made to the act next session to wipe out that injustice.

I want to reinforce, if I may, the remarks that have just been made by the member for Ontario. I raised* this question the other night when the estimates of the Postmaster General were up. I am not concerned now so much with the man who is dismissed as I am with the man who voluntarily resigns from a position in the civil service. I Was told by the Postmaster General that if a man had been in the service two years, he would get his money back if he resigned, but upon inquiry I find that that is not the case. I was talking only yesterday to a man who had been in the employ of the government for four years and had been paying into the superannuation fund. He resigned to go into another business. There was not a single thing against him, but when he applied to have the money refunded that he had paid in, it was refused. Now for the life of me I cannot see how any government can justify an action of that kind. I should like to ask the minister whose statement is correct.
Under the act the man has to have ten years' service before we oan pay back what he has paid into the fund. The law would have to be changed to meet my hon. friend's wishes.

That is the information I got from the man himself. The deputy of the Postmaster General also told me that the other night. But surely this parliament cannot justify such a thing. You take the man's money while he fe serving the people of

Supply-National Revenue
Canada, and then when, he resigns to go into another occupation you keep his money. It is absolute robbery.
It is legalized robbery.
What does the minister think about it?

I have expressed my opinion upon the point already, Mr. Chairman. I am in agreement with what the bon. gentleman gays. I do not think that even the limitation of ten years should apply, but it is so provided in the act evolved by a committee of this house. I say quite frankly that I think any man who has paid out of his wages towards the superannuation fund, and is dismissed from the service, no matter for what reason, has a good moral claim for the return of his money.

Mr. Chairman, it is only fair to say that the matter has been before the treasury board on numerous occasions, and always we have been referred to the report of the committee which evolved the present Civil Service Superannuation Act. I think the act came into force before the present government took office, but that has nothing to do with the matter, because the whole house interested itself in that legislation. It has been pointed out to us that if the principle of giving back contributions to the superannuation fund in the case of resignations up to the ten-year period were recognized, it would operate to change the scale of the contributions generally, and that scale would have to be increased to make up for those refunds. I am not arguing the question, I am merely putting before the committee the information conveyed to the members of the present treasury board as to the origin of the practice under the Superannuation Act. Personally, I hold the view that as a matter of justice it is pretty hard to take away from a man the contributions which he makes to such a fund. I draw some distinction between the man who is dismissed and the man who voluntarily resigns.
So do I.

He resigns voluntarily to better himself; but for the man who is dismissed and is thereby deprived entirely of the opportunity of benefiting from his contributions to the superannuation fund, a good deal is to be said in favour of some further consideration being given to him. But I am sure some members on both sides of the house will recall that the actuarial basis of the fund was very carefully examined by the committee at the time the act was drafted.

I appreciate, Mr. Chairman, the frankness of the minister's opinion. But surely this parliament cannot hide behind the excuse that because some committee made a wrong recommendation to this house on one occasion this injustice is to be continued. Surely it does not lie in the mouth of a minister of the crown charged with the duty of administering this department to say: We retain counsel to prosecute violators of the law, and we are helpless because they are not successful in doing so. It seems to me elementary that those who find that their instructions are not carried out should at least have the enterprise and the courage to retain counsel who will do what they are required to do, and bring before the courts the matters with which they are entrusted. So I say that the explanation which the minister has been good enough to give, while it does indeed testify to the energy he has shown and to the good he has accomplished, shows that we have but begun to remedy the abuses that existed in that department, and that we are very far from being able to congratulate ourselves upon having made any real progress down to this date.

Mr. Chairman, in view of certain statements that have been made, I may be allowed to say to the committee what is the practice in regard to these cases. As the committee is aware, the legal work of all the departments of the government extends throughout the Dominion. It has always been the practice to have legal agents in all parts of Canada, because almost every day some department asks for the name of a legal representative in some district to institute proceedings. This is done for the Department of National Revenue as well as for the other departments. It is indeed under those circumstances necessary that there should be in the department a list of legal men who could be employed in any part of Canada for this sort of work. When I became the head of the Department of Justice I found there a list of legal men practising in all parts of the Dominion to whom legal work of the various departments could be entrusted. Obviously that list had been prepared by my predecessor in office, and I had no reason to doubt the qualifications of those legal men; indeed I knew many of them personally. The names of the men who were suggested or recommended or given to the various departments were always taken from that li^t, and as far as possible those
who were more especially qualified for the kind of work which had to be done were always selected.
Now, that list existed in the deparment until 1926, when we went out of office for some time. When two or three months afterwards I came back again as the head of the department I found that that list had disappeared altogether and had been replaced by another list which I now have in my hand. There was a list for every one of the provinces, and not one of the names that were there three months previously appeared in this new list. It may be interesting to my hon. friend from Vancouver-[DOT]
